extracted.intended_audience: authors of research software preparing submissions to the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and gates for preparing and submitting a software-focused short paper and associated repository to JOSS, including technical, licensing, documentation, development-history, and review-process requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open source license (OSI-approved)
rubrics_metrics.description: The software must be open source as per the OSI definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an OSI-approved open source license in the repository before submission; the Submission Process reiterates making your software available in an open repository and include an OSI approved open source license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly browsable and clonable repository
rubrics_metrics.description: The software must be hosted at a location where users can browse the source code files, open issues, and propose code changes without manual approval of (or payment for) accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repository must be clonable without registration, source files browsable online without registration, have an issue tracker readable without registration, and permit individuals to create issues/file tickets against your repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious research application / in-scope software
rubrics_metrics.description: The software must have an obvious research application (e.g., solves complex modeling problems in scientific contexts, supports research instruments, extracts knowledge from large datasets, provides mathematical libraries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While useful for many areas, pre-trained machine learning models and notebooks are not in-scope for JOSS. Examples: physics, mathematics, biology, medicine, social science, neuroscience, engineering. The software should represent a meaningful contribution to research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitter is a major contributor
rubrics_metrics.description: You must be a major contributor to the software you are submitting and have a GitHub account to participate in the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures authors can respond to issues and participate in the public, repository-based review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper must not focus on new research results
rubrics_metrics.description: Your paper must not focus on new research results accomplished with the software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS papers are about the software itself, its design and implementation, not reporting novel scientific results produced by using the software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper hosted in a Git-based repository with software
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper (paper.md and BibTeX files, plus any figures) must be hosted in a Git-based repository together with your software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper may be in a short-lived branch which is never merged, but that branch should be created from the default so it includes the source code; use the filename paper.md and follow the example paper to match correct format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository accessibility gates (cloneable, browsable, issueable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repository must be stored where it can be cloned without registration, source files browsable online without registration, issue tracker readable without registration, and permit individuals to create issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are practical checks so reviewers can inspect, run, and interact with the project during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-complete and appropriate packaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Software should be feature-complete (i.e., no half-baked solutions) and packaged appropriately according to community standards for the programming language being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the package for maintainable extension rather than one-off modifications. “Minor utility” packages, thin API clients, and single-function packages are not acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-documented, tested, and maintainable
rubrics_metrics.description: Software should be well-documented, contain procedures (such as automated tests) for checking correctness, and be designed for maintainable extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include comprehensive documentation, tests and CI; demonstrate how correctness is validated. The Submission Process explicitly notes these as expectations when complying with the JOSS review criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope & significance — Research impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate evidence that the software is being used for research, such as references in published papers or preprints, DOIs linking to the software, documented adoption by other research groups, or clear integration into research workflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspirational statements about future use are not sufficient; concrete evidence (citations, DOIs, adoption) is required to demonstrate impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope & significance — Design thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess meaningful architectural decisions and trade-offs; value work that builds upon or extends existing software ecosystems rather than reinventing quality alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe problem framing, key design decisions, and architectural choices that make the software usable and sustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope & significance — Open development practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate sustained development over time with evidence of collaborative effort, public development history, comprehensive testing, clear documentation, and pathways for community contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects showing evidence of open development from early stages are particularly valued; public issues, pull requests, and visible history are positive indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope & significance — Usability and testability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether a potential user can easily install, understand, and test the software; if new, ensure a colleague has tried it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical installability and the ability for reviewers to run tests locally are important evaluation factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope & significance — Likelihood to be cited
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the software is sufficiently useful that it is likely to be cited by other researchers in the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of adoption, integration, or benchmarks that demonstrate near-term significance strengthens this signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review gate: Sufficient public development history (>6 months)
rubrics_metrics.description: The repository must have been public for more than six months prior to submission, with active development spanning that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated checks on commit distribution are run; a repo dump (bulk upload) or a history concentrated into a few days/weeks will not be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review gate: Demonstrated research impact
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be evidence that the software is being used for research—at minimum by the developers themselves and ideally by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable signals include references in papers, DOIs, documented adoption or clear integration into research workflows; aspirational claims are insufficient. Failure leads to desk rejection (but may be 'not yet').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review gate: Good open-source practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The repository must show active use of open-source workflows (issues, pull requests, public discussion); for single-author projects require multiple indicators of openness (commit history, tagged releases/changelog, tests, CI, documentation, CONTRIBUTING file, stated support/governance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A solo project that is otherwise open and well-maintained will not be rejected solely for lacking a PR workflow; conversely, a single-author project lacking these signals is not ready. Failure to meet this gate results in desk rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-review gate: Iterative development over time
rubrics_metrics.description: The development history must show ongoing iteration, not a single burst of commits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that the software has been refined through use and feedback over time is required; concentrated windows of significant work are a negative signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong positive signal: Community engagement beyond authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-author issues, pull requests, or discussions are a strong positive signal of a healthy open project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not a gate but counts in the submission’s favour during evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI usage policy — Author disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must disclose generative AI use in an 'AI usage disclosure' statement including tools/models used (and versions) and where they were used (code, paper text, docs); the nature and scope of assistance; and assert that humans reviewed, edited, validated all AI-assisted outputs and made core design decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI is not allowed for conversational interactions between authors and editors/reviewers except for translation. Authors remain fully responsible for accuracy, originality, licensing, and compliance. Failure to provide complete/accurate disclosure may be considered an ethical breach and can lead to desk rejection, mandatory revisions, post-publication correction or withdrawal, and potential notification of institutions/funders in cases of intentional misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI usage policy — Reviewer AI use and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may use generative AI to assist with non-substantive tasks (e.g., grammar checks, contextualizing public materials and code snippets) but must disclose this briefly at the end of their review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer—not the AI—owns the evaluation. All judgements, recommendations, and technical claims must be the reviewer’s and verified by them.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI usage policy — Human-only evaluative judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: All evaluative decisions—scoring, accept/reject recommendations, and assessments of originality, novelty, correctness, significance, and policy/ethics compliance—must be made by the human reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI tools may assist with analysis but must not render or determine any verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web-based software criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Many web-based research tools are out of scope due to lack of modularity and testing challenges; web-based tools may be in scope if they are built around and expose a 'core library' or demonstrate a high level of rigor in domain modeling and testing (e.g., adopt/implement design patterns such as MVC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is essential that any web-based tool can be tested easily by reviewers locally (on their machine). Examples: Shiny apps exposing an R library, Django app using MVC patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-publication criterion — implementation reflects scientific effort
rubrics_metrics.description: If co-publishing a JOSS paper alongside a science/methods paper, the implementation of the software itself must reflect a substantial scientific effort (design of software, implementation of algorithms, creation of tutorials, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should indicate whether related publications (published, in review, or near submission) exist when submitting to JOSS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest (COI) and disclosure policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must disclose any potential conflicts of interest (financial, personal, or professional) at submission time and acknowledge sources of financial support and whether sponsors were involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reviewers must be informed of potential COI before reviewing. Non-compliance may lead to rejection or retraction; the COI policy will be reviewed and updated regularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship eligibility and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely financial or organizational contributions are not sufficient for co-authorship; active project direction and non-code contributions can merit authorship. Co-authors must agree to be listed and be accountable for all aspects of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must notify JOSS if retractions or corrections are needed after publication. In event of a name change request the DOI remains unchanged and the paper will be updated without publishing a correction notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submissions using proprietary development environments
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS strongly prefers software that doesn’t rely upon proprietary development environments/languages, but will consider submissions that meet requirements (including valid open source license).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accepted, authors may be asked to help find reviewers who already have the required proprietary environment installed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission mechanics and required files
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you submit: make your software available in an open repo, include an OSI-approved license, ensure the software complies with JOSS review criteria (full-featured, well-documented, automated tests), and write a short paper in Markdown named paper.md including title, summary, author names, affiliations, and key references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optional: create a metadata file describing your software; a provided script can automate metadata generation. Submission is via a short submission form and then the managing editor will start a pre-review issue in the JOSS reviews repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: No submission fees
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no fees for submitting or publishing in JOSS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See JOSS cost and sustainability model for more details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review process — editor and reviewer assignment & public review
rubrics_metrics.description: An Associate Editor-in-Chief will do an initial check and assign a handling editor, who will assign two or more JOSS reviewers. The review is carried out in the JOSS reviews repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews are iterative and conversational. Reviewer and editor contributions should be acknowledged in the repository. Authors respond to reviewer-raised issues on the submission repository’s issue tracker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review process — author responsiveness timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are expected to respond to reviewer comments and questions promptly—generally within 2 weeks—and complete requested changes within 4–6 weeks, unless otherwise negotiated with the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need more time, communicate via the review thread. Prolonged unresponsiveness may result in rejection due to lack of engagement. Allow a week for an editor to respond before prompting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-acceptance release and archiving requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon successful completion of the review, authors must make a tagged release of the software, deposit a copy of the repository with a data-archiving service (e.g., Zenodo or figshare), obtain a DOI for the archive, and update the review issue thread with the version number and DOI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After JOSS assigns a DOI for the accepted paper, metadata is deposited with CrossRef and listed on the JOSS website; the review issue will be closed and an announcement posted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of reviewer and editor contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer and editor contributions, like any other contributions, should be acknowledged in the repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat review and editorial contributions as citable/acknowledgable contributions to the project.
